title: Holy Saturday
hookLine: the tabernacle open and empty, the church stripped
last: BEHOLD THE WOOD OF THE CROSS.

lines: A DAY WITH ALMOST NOTHING ON IT.
cards: Holy Thursday has a supper. Good Friday has a cross. Easter has an empty tomb.

In between sits a whole day with almost nothing on it. No Mass from morning until nightfall. The tabernacle stands open and empty, as it was left yesterday, and in many parishes the holy water fonts by the door are dry.
Somebody might be arranging lilies in a side room for tonight, but out in the church, nothing happens. On purpose.

teach.b: The Gospels say very little about this day, and that silence is the point. Matthew tells us the authorities sealed the stone and set guards.
Luke gives one plain sentence about the women who had watched the burial, in the Douay-Rheims: "And on the sabbath day they rested, according to the commandment."
The women who loved him most spent the day keeping the sabbath, with spices waiting in a jar for Sunday morning. They were not waiting for a resurrection. They were waiting to anoint a body.
So the Church keeps the day the way they did: nothing added.

teach.h: THE CHURCH WAITS AT THE TOMB.
teach.b: The Missal says the Church waits at the Lord's tomb, praying and fasting, and the altar stays bare. The empty tabernacle is the loudest sign of all.

The consecrated hosts were moved from the main altar on Thursday night, given out at Friday's service, and any left over taken to a quiet place apart; Christ's presence, in the way Catholics speak of it, is not kept in the church today.
But Catholics don't say the day is empty of him.
The Apostles' Creed says he descended into hell, and Catholic teaching is that he went down among the dead, to the righteous who had waited since Adam, to bring them out.
An ancient homily for this day, read in the Church's Office of Readings, pictures him taking Adam by the hand. On earth, a great silence.

teach.h: AND ON THE SABBATH DAY THEY RESTED.
teach.b: Underneath it, something is happening that nobody can see yet. That's the shape of a lot of real waiting: a hospital corridor, an inbox, a hard year.
Holy Saturday gives that feeling a place in the calendar, and doesn't rush it.

how: On Holy Saturday Catholic churches keep the altar bare and the tabernacle empty, no Mass is celebrated during the day, and many Catholics fast, pray quietly, or visit the church before the Easter Vigil after nightfall.

o: the day the Last Supper is remembered in church
the morning the risen Jesus first appeared
the quiet day of waiting at the tomb before Easter

games.q: what the church looks like today — tap the pairs.
p: rested on the sabbath, spices ready

s: Mass is celebrated as usual on Holy Saturday morning
no Mass is said during the day. the next Mass is the Easter Vigil, after nightfall.
on Holy Saturday the tabernacle is left open and empty
the Eucharist was moved on Holy Thursday night and given out or kept apart after Good Friday; the open door is the sign.
the Gospels describe what the disciples did all day Saturday
they say almost nothing: a sealed stone, guards, and women who rested according to the commandment.

games.q: you're one of the women who watched the burial. it's the sabbath, and the spices are ready. what do you do?
o: go to the tomb at once with the spices.
rest, as the commandment says, and wait for Sunday.
leave Jerusalem and go home to Galilee.
games.why: Luke says they rested on the sabbath, according to the commandment, and came at dawn on Sunday. they were waiting to anoint a body, not expecting Easter.

practice: Sit somewhere still with your phone face down: near the open tabernacle if you can reach a church, or a parked car, a bench, the edge of your bed.
Think of one thing in your life you're still waiting on, and let it stay unresolved for a while, without praying or planning. If you pray, you can simply stay, the way the women stayed.

wordCard.voice: Holy Saturday. The day between the cross and Easter: a bare altar, an empty tabernacle, no Mass, and the Church waiting at the tomb. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: Holy Saturday, the great sabbath of the Church's year.

carryVoice: Your line: the day of waiting. The spices are ready; Sunday hasn't come yet. Day six hundred sixty-two.
